groups.title: Lakes of the Lake District
groups.explanation: Each is a lake in the Cumbrian fells, and Windermere is the largest in England.

groups.title: Romantic poets
groups.explanation: All four wrote in the Romantic years at the turn of the nineteenth century.

groups.title: Cumbrian fells
groups.explanation: Each is a fell walked from the valleys of the Lake District.

sources.excerpt: They include Windermere, which with a length of 11 miles (18 km) and an area of 5.69 square miles (14.73 km2) is the longest and largest lake in England, and Wast Water, which at 79 metres (259 ft) is the deepest lake in England.
Coniston Water is a lake in the Lake District in North West England.
It is the third largest by volume, after Windermere and Ullswater, and the fifth-largest by area.
Buttermere is a lake in the Lake District in North West England.
They were associated with several other poets and writers, including Dorothy Wordsworth, Charles Lamb, Mary Lamb, Charles Lloyd, Hartley Coleridge, John Wilson, and Thomas De Quincey.
Keats had a style "heavily loaded with sensualities", notably in the series of odes.
John Keats (31 October 1795 – 23 February 1821) was an English poet of the second generation of Romantic poets, along with Lord Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley.
The Lakeland fells, or mountains, include England's highest: Scafell Pike (978 m; 3,209 ft), Helvellyn (950 m; 3,120 ft) and Skiddaw (931 m; 3,054 ft).
Blencathra, also known as Saddleback, is one of the most northerly of the Cumbrian Mountains, in the English Lake District.

editorNotes: Coniston is the tile that fits twice, a lake and the fell above it known as the Old Man of Coniston; the fell group is complete with Helvellyn, Skiddaw, Blencathra and Scafell Pike, so Coniston is counted as a lake. Windermere and Buttermere are villages as well as lakes, but no group here asks for villages, and Wordsworth lived at Grasmere, which was left out for that reason.
